patient.name: Chloe Brennan
patient.complaint: Eight months of bloating, loose pale stools and tiredness, with an itchy rash on her elbows
background: Older sister diagnosed with coeliac disease last year
Hoping to start a family next year

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with chronic non-bloody diarrhoea, bloating, fatigue and a mixed anaemia (low ferritin and folate, MCV often normal) in someone with autoimmune thyroid disease or type 1 diabetes, or an itchy extensor rash (dermatitis herpetiformis).

points: Chloe, 27: **bloating** worse after bread and pasta.
Loose, **pale, foul-smelling** stools that are hard to flush.
No blood. Tired for months; 4 kg lost.
Her sister has **coeliac disease**; she has **Hashimoto's**.

steps.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
steps.r: Chronic non-bloody diarrhoea, **steatorrhoea**, symptoms after gluten, an autoimmune thyroid and a sister with coeliac: **coeliac disease**.

steps.lead: Chloe's gut is reacting to **gluten**: a T-cell-mediated autoimmune attack that flattens the small bowel villi and causes **malabsorption**.
Chloe has two risk factors: a **first-degree relative** and **autoimmune thyroid disease**. NICE says test anyone newly diagnosed with either.

points: Clusters of tiny, scratched **blisters on both elbows** and buttocks.

steps.lead: Chloe has the classic picture: chronic **non-bloody** diarrhoea, **steatorrhoea**, bloating after bread, fatigue, weight loss, pallor and **koilonychia** from iron deficiency.
The itchy blisters on Chloe's elbows and buttocks are **dermatitis herpetiformis**: specific enough to point straight to coeliac disease.
If Chloe stays undiagnosed or eats gluten, she risks **EATL**, small bowel adenocarcinoma and **osteoporosis**.

steps.text: A **normal MCV** does not exclude coeliac anaemia. Iron (microcytic) plus folate (macrocytic) deficiency can average out, so look at the **RDW**.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' (total IgA plus IgA tTG, while eating gluten), the IgA deficiency trap (use IgG tTG), the gold standard (duodenal biopsy) and the classic findings (villous atrophy, Howell-Jolly bodies).

steps.q: What is the first-line test for Chloe?
steps.r: **Serology first**: total IgA plus IgA tTG. Biopsy confirms after a positive result.

steps.lead: Chloe is still eating gluten, so her **total IgA and IgA tTG** will be valid. Total IgA is checked because **IgA deficiency** gives a false negative.

steps.title: Chloe's coeliac serology
steps.text: Normal total IgA, so the strongly positive tTG is believable.

visual.title: IgA anti-tTG
visual.label: Chloe 128
visual.caption: Very high tTG makes coeliac disease very likely; she is referred for OGD and biopsy.

steps.text: If Chloe had already gone **gluten free**, her tests could be falsely negative. She must eat gluten for **at least 6 weeks** before serology.

visual.title: Gluten challenge before testing
bands: Too short: risk of false negative
visual.label: Chloe: never stopped
visual.caption: Eat gluten in more than one meal a day for at least 6 weeks.

steps.title: Chloe's other bloods
steps.text: Mixed iron and folate deficiency: normal MCV, high RDW.

steps.lead: Chloe's **mixed deficiency** gives a normal MCV with a **high RDW**; **Howell-Jolly bodies** mean hyposplenism.

steps.title: Chloe's diagnostic pathway
nodes: Total IgA + IgA tTG while eating gluten
Villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, IELs → confirmed
steps.caption: If IgA deficient, use IgG tTG instead.

steps.lead: Chloe's **OGD** shows scalloped, flattened duodenal folds; biopsies show **sub-total villous atrophy**, crypt hyperplasia and intra-epithelial lymphocytes.
Chloe has a baseline **DEXA** scan for bone density, and her tTG will be repeated to track response.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate management?' where the answer is a lifelong strict gluten-free diet, with dapsone for dermatitis herpetiformis, iron and folate replacement, 5 mg folic acid in pregnancy and pneumococcal vaccination for hyposplenism.

points: She asks: 'Is it just until I feel better?'

steps.lead: Chloe's only definitive treatment is **lifelong** gluten exclusion: no wheat, barley or rye; rice, potatoes and corn are safe.

steps.q: Chloe's elbow rash is still itchy despite the diet. What should be added?
steps.r: **Dapsone** controls dermatitis herpetiformis while the gluten-free diet takes months to work.

steps.lead: Chloe takes **dapsone** for her rash with a strict gluten-free diet, plus **iron and folate** to correct her anaemia.
Chloe has hyposplenism, so she gets a **pneumococcal vaccine every 5 years**. As she plans pregnancy, she takes **folic acid 5 mg** until 12 weeks.

visual.title: Chloe on a gluten-free diet
visual.caption: A falling tTG is the best marker of adherence; it should normalise by about 12 months.

steps.lead: Had Chloe arrived with **severe diarrhoea and weight loss**, coeliac disease should still be considered and she would need urgent assessment.
Chloe's sister's diagnosis and Chloe's thyroid disease fit **NICE**: test for coeliac in new autoimmune thyroid disease or type 1 diabetes.

steps.text: Poor adherence is the main risk for **EATL**. A treated patient with new weight loss, pain or night sweats needs investigation, not reassurance.
Never tell a patient to try a gluten-free diet **before** testing: it makes the serology and biopsy falsely negative.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: the HLA association (DQ2/DQ8), the role of tissue transglutaminase, why fat and iron are malabsorbed, why hyposplenism needs pneumococcal vaccine, and why DH responds to diet.

steps.lead: Chloe carries the susceptibility genes **HLA-DQ2/DQ8**; **gliadin** from her bread is deamidated by **tTG**, making it more immunogenic.

steps.title: From bread to flat villi
nodes: HLA-DQ2/DQ8 presents it to T cells
steps.caption: The same tTG is the target of the antibody test.

steps.lead: Chloe's flat villi explain everything: less **surface area**, so poor fat (steatorrhoea), iron, folate and calcium absorption.

steps.q: Why are Chloe's stools pale and hard to flush?
steps.r: Villous atrophy stops fat being absorbed: **steatorrhoea** is bulky, pale, offensive and floats.

steps.lead: Chloe's **Howell-Jolly bodies** reflect hyposplenism, so she is vulnerable to **encapsulated organisms** like the pneumococcus.
Chloe's rash is **IgA immune complexes** in the dermis, driven by gluten, so it settles with a gluten-free diet.
Years of untreated T-cell inflammation is what raises Chloe's risk of **EATL**; strict diet lowers it.

steps.text: Duodenal biopsy shows **villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia and intra-epithelial lymphocytes**: all three come from the T-cell attack.

glossary.coeliac disease: Autoimmune small bowel disease triggered by gluten, causing villous atrophy and malabsorption.
glossary.gluten: Protein in wheat, barley and rye that triggers coeliac disease.
glossary.gliadin: The part of gluten that the immune system reacts to in coeliac disease.
glossary.tTG: Tissue transglutaminase: the enzyme that deamidates gliadin and the target of coeliac antibodies.
glossary.tissue transglutaminase: Enzyme that modifies gliadin, making it more immunogenic; the antigen in the coeliac blood test.
glossary.anti-tTG: Antibodies against tissue transglutaminase; IgA anti-tTG is the first-line coeliac test.
glossary.anti-endomysial antibodies: IgA antibodies against the connective tissue around smooth muscle; highly specific for coeliac disease.
glossary.IgA deficiency: Low or absent IgA, commoner in coeliac disease, causing false-negative IgA antibody tests.
glossary.deamidation: Chemical change of glutamine to glutamate that makes gliadin bind HLA-DQ2/DQ8 more strongly.
glossary.HLA-DQ2: The main genetic susceptibility allele for coeliac disease.
glossary.HLA-DQ8: The second genetic susceptibility allele for coeliac disease.
glossary.villous atrophy: Flattening of the finger-like villi of the small bowel, cutting absorptive surface area.
glossary.crypt hyperplasia: Lengthening of intestinal crypts as the lining tries to regenerate.
glossary.intra-epithelial lymphocytes: T cells within the gut lining; increased numbers are the earliest coeliac change.
glossary.OGD: Oesophago-gastro-duodenoscopy: camera test of the upper gut used to take duodenal biopsies.
glossary.scalloping: A notched, saw-tooth look to the duodenal folds at endoscopy, seen in coeliac disease.
glossary.malabsorption: Failure to absorb nutrients from the gut, causing deficiencies and weight loss.
glossary.steatorrhoea: Pale, bulky, offensive, greasy stools that float, from fat malabsorption.
glossary.koilonychia: Spoon-shaped nails, a sign of iron deficiency.
glossary.osteomalacia: Soft bones from poor mineralisation, usually due to vitamin D deficiency.
glossary.dermatitis herpetiformis: Intensely itchy blistering rash on extensor surfaces, specific to coeliac disease.
glossary.DH: Dermatitis herpetiformis: the itchy blistering skin manifestation of coeliac disease.
glossary.papulovesicular: Describes a rash of small raised bumps and tiny fluid-filled blisters.
glossary.dapsone: An antibacterial drug that rapidly controls the itch of dermatitis herpetiformis.
glossary.EATL: Enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma: a non-Hodgkin lymphoma of the small bowel complicating coeliac disease.
glossary.non-Hodgkin lymphoma: A group of lymphomas without Reed-Sternberg cells, including EATL.
glossary.adenocarcinoma: Cancer arising from glandular epithelium, here of the small bowel.
glossary.hyposplenism: Reduced spleen function, raising the risk of infection with encapsulated bacteria.
glossary.Howell-Jolly bodies: Nuclear fragments in red cells seen on the blood film when the spleen is not working.
glossary.encapsulated organisms: Bacteria with a sugar capsule, such as pneumococcus, normally cleared by the spleen.
glossary.RDW: Red cell distribution width: a high value means red cells vary widely in size.
glossary.MCV: Mean cell volume: the average red cell size, used to classify anaemia.
glossary.ferritin: Iron storage protein; a low level confirms iron deficiency.
glossary.macrocytic: Large red cells (high MCV), seen in B12 or folate deficiency.
glossary.DEXA: Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry: a scan measuring bone mineral density.
glossary.osteoporosis: Low bone density with a raised risk of fracture.
glossary.gluten challenge: Eating gluten daily for at least 6 weeks so that tests can be interpreted.
glossary.Hashimoto's: Autoimmune thyroiditis causing hypothyroidism; linked to coeliac disease.
glossary.Graves' disease: Autoimmune hyperthyroidism; linked to coeliac disease.
glossary.faecal calprotectin: A stool marker of bowel inflammation, raised in IBD but not IBS.
glossary.giardiasis: Infection with Giardia lamblia, causing greasy diarrhoea and bloating after drinking untreated water.

technique.stem: A 34 year old woman with Graves' disease treated with carbimazole has a 6 month history of bloating, loose stools and tiredness. Her symptoms are worse after eating pasta. There is no blood in her stools. She has lost 3 kg.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question about chronic diarrhoea.
Autoimmune thyroid disease, non-bloody chronic diarrhoea, gluten-linked bloating, weight loss.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Coeliac disease.

elim: Usually bloody or painful diarrhoea with raised inflammatory markers; no autoimmune link given.
Weight loss is a red flag that does not fit IBS.
Symptoms follow dairy, not pasta, and weight loss is unusual.
Needs travel or untreated water exposure, and would not explain the autoimmune link.

steps.x: **A. Coeliac disease.** Rule: autoimmune disease + chronic non-bloody diarrhoea = test for coeliac.

technique.stem: A 22 year old man has had bloating and diarrhoea for a year. After reading online he stopped eating gluten 3 months ago and feels much better. His IgA anti-tTG is negative and his total IgA is normal. He wants to know whether he has coeliac disease.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Reintroduce gluten for 6 weeks, then repeat serology

steps.x: 'Next step' after a negative test.
He has been gluten free, so the negative test is unreliable.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Gluten challenge for at least 6 weeks, then repeat serology.

elim: Only for IgA deficiency; his total IgA is normal.
Biopsy will also be falsely normal on a gluten-free diet.
A positive HLA type is common and does not confirm disease.
The test is invalid on a gluten-free diet.

steps.x: **E.** Rule: no gluten, no valid test.

technique.stem: A 40 year old man was diagnosed with coeliac disease 2 years ago and follows a strict gluten-free diet. His tTG has normalised. His blood film shows Howell-Jolly bodies. He has had no vaccines since childhood.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate additional management?

steps.x: Additional management in established coeliac disease.
Howell-Jolly bodies = hyposplenism = encapsulated organism risk.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Pneumococcal vaccine, repeated every 5 years.

elim: For dermatitis herpetiformis, which he does not have.
Not routine for coeliac hyposplenism; vaccination is the step.
No anaemia is described.
His spleen already works poorly; removing it makes no sense.

steps.x: **D. Pneumococcal vaccine.** Rule: coeliac hyposplenism needs 5-yearly pneumococcal vaccination.

technique.stem: A 29 year old woman with untreated coeliac disease has pale, bulky, offensive stools that are difficult to flush. Duodenal biopsy shows sub-total villous atrophy with crypt hyperplasia.
technique.q: Which best explains the character of her stools?
o: Bile acid malabsorption from ileal disease
Reduced mucosal surface area for fat absorption

steps.x: A mechanism question explaining a symptom.
Steatorrhoea plus flat villi.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Villous atrophy reduces surface area, so fat is not absorbed.

elim: There is no surgical blind loop.
Coeliac disease affects the proximal small bowel.
That causes watery secretory diarrhoea, not steatorrhoea.
Her pancreas is normal; the problem is the mucosa.

steps.x: **E.** Rule: flat villi = less surface = steatorrhoea and deficiencies.

practice.stem: A 31 year old woman has a 9 month history of tiredness, bloating and loose, pale stools. Her mother has type 1 diabetes. Her temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 92 bpm and BP 110/70 mmHg. She has pale conjunctivae.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Chronic non-bloody diarrhoea with mixed iron and folate deficiency (normal MCV, high RDW) and an autoimmune family history is coeliac disease. IBS does not cause anaemia.

steps.x: Diagnosis with blood results.

clues: tiredness, bloating and loose, pale stools
steps.x: Malabsorption pattern: low ferritin and folate with a normal MCV and high RDW (mixed deficiency).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Coeliac disease.

elim: Would raise CRP and usually causes pain or bloody stools.
Needs a travel or water exposure history.
Causes constipation and does not cause low ferritin and folate together.
Bloods are normal in IBS; anaemia excludes it.

steps.x: **A. Coeliac disease.** Mixed iron and folate deficiency + chronic diarrhoea.

practice.stem: A 25 year old man has a 3 month history of an intensely itchy rash. There are grouped small blisters and excoriations on both elbows, knees and buttocks. He has occasional loose stools and bloating. He is otherwise well.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Intensely itchy grouped papulovesicles on extensor surfaces with bloating and loose stools are dermatitis herpetiformis, the specific skin sign of coeliac disease.

steps.x: A skin diagnosis with a GI clue.
Itchy grouped vesicles on **extensors** with GI symptoms.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Dermatitis herpetiformis, the skin manifestation of coeliac disease.

elim: Affects flexures, without grouped vesicles on extensors.
Large tense blisters in the elderly.
Silvery scaly plaques, not itchy grouped blisters.
Burrows in finger webs and wrists, with itchy contacts.

steps.x: **C. Dermatitis herpetiformis.** Extensor itchy blisters + gut symptoms = coeliac.

practice.stem: A 9 year old boy with type 1 diabetes has had recurrent unexplained hypoglycaemia, abdominal bloating and loose stools for 6 months. He has fallen from the 50th to the 25th centile for weight. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 98/60 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Coeliac disease is associated with type 1 diabetes; malabsorption causes unexplained hypoglycaemia, bloating and faltering growth. NICE advises testing at diabetes diagnosis.

steps.x: Diagnosis in a child with type 1 diabetes.
Malabsorption in a type 1 diabetic: poor absorption of carbohydrate causes hypos; faltering growth.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Coeliac disease.

elim: Causes hypoglycaemia but with pigmentation and hypotension, not steatorrhoea and bloating.
Starts in infancy.
Rare in children; gives vomiting and early satiety.
Does not cause falling growth or hypoglycaemia.

steps.x: **B. Coeliac disease.** Rule: type 1 diabetes + GI symptoms or unexplained hypos = test for coeliac.

practice.stem: A 58 year old man diagnosed with coeliac disease 20 years ago admits he rarely follows a gluten-free diet. He has 2 months of abdominal pain, night sweats and 8 kg weight loss. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 98 bpm, BP 118/72 mmHg and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. CT shows thickened jejunal loops with mesenteric lymphadenopathy.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Poorly controlled long-standing coeliac disease with B symptoms and thickened jejunum is enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma, a non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a complication.

clues: night sweats and 8 kg weight loss
thickened jejunal loops with mesenteric lymphadenopathy
steps.x: Long-standing poorly controlled coeliac, B symptoms, small bowel thickening.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: EATL.

elim: New Crohn's at 58 is less likely, and the coeliac history with non-adherence points to lymphoma.
Linked to H. pylori and the stomach, not the jejunum.
Nodal disease with Reed-Sternberg cells, not a small bowel lymphoma.
Would not explain night sweats, fever and nodal masses.

steps.x: **B. EATL.** Rule: known coeliac + weight loss + sweats = lymphoma until proven otherwise.

practice.stem: A 36 year old woman with long-standing coeliac disease is reviewed in clinic. She is tired. She has never had a splenectomy. A full blood count and blood film are sent.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on the blood film?
practice.e: Coeliac disease causes hyposplenism, so the spleen fails to remove nuclear remnants: Howell-Jolly bodies. Thrombocytosis can also occur.

steps.x: 'Most likely finding' on a film in coeliac disease.
Coeliac causes functional hyposplenism.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Howell-Jolly bodies.

elim: Seen in G6PD deficiency with oxidant stress.
Seen with high immunoglobulins, e.g. myeloma.
Fragmented cells in haemolysis such as DIC or TTP.
Hereditary spherocytosis or autoimmune haemolysis.

steps.x: **B. Howell-Jolly bodies.** Coeliac hyposplenism leaves nuclear remnants in red cells.

practice.stem: A 28 year old man has a positive IgA anti-tTG of 96 U/mL (<7) with a normal total IgA. He is still eating gluten. He undergoes gastroscopy and duodenal biopsies are taken.
practice.q: Which is the most likely histological finding?
o: Crypt abscesses and goblet cell depletion
Villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia and intra-epithelial lymphocytes
practice.e: Coeliac disease shows sub-total villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia and increased intra-epithelial lymphocytes. Granulomas suggest Crohn's; PAS-positive macrophages suggest Whipple's.

steps.x: 'Most likely finding' on biopsy.
Strong serology while on gluten: biopsy will show the classic triad.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, intra-epithelial lymphocytes.

elim: The pattern of ulcerative colitis.
Suggests Crohn's disease or sarcoidosis.
Whipple's disease.
Giardiasis.

steps.x: **E.** Rule: coeliac histology = flat villi, deep crypts, lots of lymphocytes.

practice.stem: A 26 year old woman with newly diagnosed autoimmune hypothyroidism has had intermittent bloating and loose stools for a year. She eats bread and pasta daily. Her temperature is 36.5°C, pulse rate 74 bpm and BP 114/72 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
practice.e: First-line testing is total IgA with IgA anti-tTG, done while eating gluten. Duodenal biopsy is the gold standard but follows positive serology.

steps.x: Initial investigation for suspected coeliac disease.
Risk group plus symptoms, and she is eating gluten.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Total IgA plus IgA anti-tTG.

elim: Not first-line for suspected coeliac disease.
The gold standard, but serology comes first.
Distinguishes IBD from IBS; not a coeliac test.
Has a negative predictive value only; not first-line.

steps.x: **E.** Rule: serology first, biopsy to confirm.

practice.stem: A 19 year old man has chronic diarrhoea, bloating and iron deficiency anaemia. He eats gluten daily. His blood results are shown.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
practice.e: He is IgA deficient, which occurs in about 2% of coeliac patients and makes the IgA anti-tTG falsely negative, so an IgG anti-tTG is measured.

steps.x: Next investigation after a negative test.
Total IgA is undetectable: IgA deficiency gives a false-negative IgA tTG.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: IgG anti-tTG.

elim: Not the next step for suspected coeliac.
Not a coeliac test.
Will be falsely negative again because he is IgA deficient.
IgA deficiency makes the negative IgA tTG unreliable.

steps.x: **C. IgG tTG.** Rule: IgA deficient → IgG-based test.

practice.stem: A 30 year old woman has coeliac disease confirmed on duodenal biopsy. She has mild iron deficiency. She asks how long she must avoid gluten. Her temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 80 bpm and BP 116/74 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Gluten-free diet for 12 months then re-challenge
practice.e: Lifelong dietary exclusion of gluten is the only definitive treatment for coeliac disease; iron is replaced alongside. Dapsone is for dermatitis herpetiformis.

steps.x: Definitive management of confirmed coeliac.

clues: how long she must avoid gluten
steps.x: Confirmed disease; the question is duration.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Lifelong strict gluten-free diet, plus iron.

elim: Gluten exclusion must be lifelong.
Re-challenge would restart the damage.
Not first-line; used only in refractory disease.
Treats dermatitis herpetiformis, not the gut disease.

steps.x: **C.** Rule: the only definitive treatment is lifelong gluten exclusion.

practice.stem: A 24 year old man with coeliac disease confirmed 2 months ago has started a gluten-free diet. He has an intensely itchy blistering rash on his elbows and buttocks that is stopping him sleeping. Skin biopsy shows granular IgA deposits in the dermal papillae.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate additional treatment?
practice.e: Dermatitis herpetiformis is treated with dapsone alongside a strict gluten-free diet, which takes months to clear the rash. G6PD is checked before dapsone.

steps.x: Additional treatment for a skin complication.
Dermatitis herpetiformis; the diet takes months.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Dapsone plus the strict gluten-free diet.

elim: For herpes infection; DH is not viral despite its name.
Used for psoriasis, not DH.
Not the treatment for DH.
Will not control DH.

steps.x: **B. Dapsone.** Rule: DH = dapsone + gluten-free diet.

practice.stem: A 32 year old woman with well-controlled coeliac disease plans to become pregnant in the next few months. She takes no medication. Her BP is 112/70 mmHg and pulse rate 72 bpm.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
o: Avoid pregnancy until tTG is undetectable for 2 years
Folic acid 400 micrograms daily until 12 weeks
Folic acid 5 mg daily until 12 weeks of pregnancy
Stop the gluten-free diet during pregnancy
practice.e: Women with coeliac disease take 5 mg folic acid daily until 12 weeks of pregnancy because folate malabsorption raises the risk of neural tube defects.

steps.x: Pre-pregnancy advice in coeliac disease.
Malabsorption of folate raises neural tube defect risk.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: High-dose folic acid, 5 mg daily, until 12 weeks.

elim: The standard dose; coeliac patients need the higher dose.
No such rule.
Malabsorption raises neural tube defect risk.
Gluten exclusion is lifelong.

steps.x: **C. 5 mg folic acid.** Rule: coeliac = high-dose folic acid in pregnancy.

practice.stem: A 23 year old woman's brother has coeliac disease. She asks why some people develop an immune reaction to gluten while others do not. Her doctor explains that deamidated gliadin binds strongly to particular antigen-presenting molecules.
practice.q: Which genetic association best explains her susceptibility?
practice.e: Tissue transglutaminase deamidates gliadin, which then binds HLA-DQ2 or DQ8 and is presented to T cells. HLA-B27 is linked to ankylosing spondylitis.

steps.x: A genetics and mechanism question.
Class II HLA presents deamidated gliadin to T cells.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: HLA-DQ2/DQ8.

elim: Linked to ankylosing spondylitis and reactive arthritis.
